reading.rtitle: The Second Market Is the Hard One
paras: Every software company that sells outside its own country tells more or less the same story about the first market and the second one. The first is usually chosen for you: a client asks, a partner introduces you, and suddenly you have landed a contract in a country you had not planned to enter. The second market is the one you choose, and it is the one that has broken more expansion plans than any spreadsheet ever has. What has changed in the last five years is not the ambition. It is the speed at which a small company can be expected to look like a large one.

The pattern is easy to see once you know where to look. A company builds up a steady base at home, wins on word of mouth, and reaches the milestone that everybody photographs: the first overseas deal. Then it expands into a second country and discovers that almost nothing travels. The product travels. The track record does not, because nobody there has heard of the clients that made it. The people who closed the first deal have never had to explain the company to a room that does not already trust it, and that turns out to be a completely different job.

There is one thing that does travel, and it is not the pitch. It is the relationship. The companies that have grown fastest outside their own market are usually the ones that treated the second country as a place to be present rather than a place to sell, and that has meant slower first years and better fifth ones. It is an uncomfortable answer for a board, because presence is hard to put on a slide. But it explains why so many expansions that looked well funded have stalled, and why some that looked small have not.

listenings.text: People always ask what the hardest part of going international is and they expect me to say the language or the taxes. It is neither. The hardest part is that you arrive with nothing. At home we have built up a track record over twelve years, we have never had to introduce ourselves, business comes through word of mouth. You land in a new country and none of that exists. I have sat in meetings where I could see the person opposite me deciding whether we were real, and I had no way to prove it except by turning up again. We have expanded into three markets now and the pattern has been identical every single time. Year one is embarrassing. Year two is slow. Year three, somebody you helped two years ago mentions your name in a room you are not in, and that is the moment it starts.

I have been in this job for nine years and I have almost never applied for anything. That sounds like luck and partly it is, but the honest version is that I have said yes to a lot of things that were not my job. The first time somebody asked me to fly out and present to a client overseas, I had never done it, I had no idea what I was doing, and I said yes on the phone before I could think about it. That was the turning point, although it did not feel like one at the time. It felt like a bad week. Since then almost every good thing has come through somebody who was in one of those rooms. My career has not been a plan. It has been a very steady accumulation of favours I said yes to.
